name: Mare Imbrium
terrain: Vast circular basaltic plain inside a 1145 km impact basin. Floor is mostly flat lava flows with subdued wrinkle ridges and a few large embedded craters (Archimedes, Aristillus, Autolycus).
composition_notes: Iron- and titanium-rich basalt with an unusually high thorium signal in the western part — overlaps with the Procellarum KREEP Terrane.
lighting_notes: Earth visible from anywhere on the floor. Sun reaches high in the lunar sky; surface gets very hot during day.
formation_notes: Imbrium impact ~3.85 Ga excavated the basin; basalt flooded the floor over the next ~500 My.
significance: One of the largest, youngest, and most-studied lunar basins. Its ejecta defines the Imbrian stratigraphic system.

name: Mare Serenitatis
terrain: Roughly circular basaltic plain with concentric mascon wrinkle ridges. Floor surface is darker than surrounding highlands; centre has a distinct dark mantling deposit.
composition_notes: Higher-titanium basalt than Mare Imbrium. Apollo 17 samples include orange-glass beads from pyroclastic fountaining.
formation_notes: Pre-Nectarian impact basin, flooded by basalt later.
significance: Apollo 17 (Taurus-Littrow valley) sampled the southeast rim. Returned the youngest mare basalts and the famous orange soil.

name: Mare Tranquillitatis
terrain: Irregular flat basaltic plain with no clear basin shape. Surface peppered with small fresh craters and crossed by low wrinkle ridges.
composition_notes: Some of the highest-titanium basalts on the Moon. Apollo 11 returned ilmenite-rich samples.
lighting_notes: Equatorial — sun passes nearly overhead at noon.
formation_notes: No clean basin; basalt fills an irregular older depression along several Imbrian-age rims.
significance: Apollo 11 (Tranquility Base) — first crewed lunar landing, 20 July 1969. Surveyor 5 robotic precursor in 1967.

name: Mare Crisium
terrain: Oval basaltic plain inside a clean 556 km impact basin near the eastern limb. Mascon causes pronounced gravity high.
composition_notes: Lower-Ti basalt. Luna 24 returned regolith samples.
lighting_notes: Near the limb; Earth low on horizon, libration changes visibility appreciably.
significance: Isolated, well-defined basin makes it a textbook example. Luna 24 (1976) sampled the southwest floor — the last Soviet sample-return mission.

name: Mare Frigoris
terrain: Long, narrow, irregular basaltic plain stretching ~1500 km east–west across the high northern latitudes. Not basin-shaped.
lighting_notes: High-latitude — sun stays low, shadows are long.
significance: One of the few non-basin maria. Borders Mare Imbrium to the south. Northern shore approaches the polar zone.

name: Oceanus Procellarum
terrain: The single largest mare. Sprawling basaltic plain covering most of the western near side. No clean basin shape.
composition_notes: Defines the Procellarum KREEP Terrane — anomalously high thorium, potassium, and rare-earth elements. Geochemically unique on the Moon.
formation_notes: Not a single impact event. The Procellarum 'super-basin' model is contested; may instead reflect a thinned crust and elevated heat flow that allowed prolonged volcanism.
significance: Site of Aristarchus crater (brightest spot on the Moon), Schroeter's Valley, Marius Hills volcanic complex, and the Apollo 12 landing.

name: Mare Nubium
terrain: Mid-southern basaltic plain. Flat, with several embedded craters and the Straight Wall (Rupes Recta) fault.
significance: Ranger 7 returned the first close-up TV images of the Moon, July 1964.

name: Mare Humorum
terrain: Small, neat circular mare in the southwest. Steep rim, concentric rilles in the surrounding highlands.

name: Mare Nectaris
terrain: Smaller basaltic mare in the southeast near side. Rim defines the Nectarian stratigraphic system.
significance: Type-locality for the Nectarian period (~3.92–3.85 Ga).

name: Mare Vaporum
terrain: Small mare just north of the equator, between Mare Imbrium and Mare Tranquillitatis. Borders the Apennine Mountains.

name: Mare Cognitum
terrain: Basaltic plain south of Copernicus. 'Sea That Has Become Known' — named after Ranger 7 deliberately impacted here.

name: Mare Marginis
terrain: Basaltic plain on the eastern limb, only fully visible during favorable libration.

name: Mare Smythii
terrain: Limb mare, equatorial. Filled with thin basalt layer over a crustal thinning.

name: Mare Australe
terrain: Highly degraded mare straddling the southeast limb. Mostly buried under highland ejecta.

name: Mare Fecunditatis
terrain: Large irregular mare in the southeast. Contains the prominent Messier crater chain.

name: Sinus Iridum
terrain: Half-circle 'bay' on the northwest edge of Mare Imbrium. Promontorium Heraclides and Promontorium Laplace cap its arms.

name: Sinus Medii
terrain: Small basaltic 'bay' near the lunar centre, almost on the 0/0 sub-Earth point.
lighting_notes: Earth always at zenith — most centred of all named features as seen from Earth.

name: Mare Moscoviense
terrain: One of the few basaltic-floored areas on the otherwise highland far side. Located in the Moscoviense impact basin.
significance: Found by Soviet Luna 3 in 1959 — first far-side imagery.

name: Mare Ingenii
terrain: Small far-side mare in the Ingenii basin. Hosts unusual swirl features (Reiner Gamma analog).

name: Mare Orientale
terrain: Multi-ringed impact basin on the western limb. The youngest and freshest large basin on the Moon — concentric rings of Cordillera and Rook Mountains preserved.
significance: Best-preserved multi-ring basin in the solar system — the type example for understanding very large impacts.

name: South Pole–Aitken basin
terrain: The largest, deepest, and oldest known impact basin in the solar system. ~2400 km across, up to 13 km deep relative to the surrounding highlands. Far-side and southern.
composition_notes: Anomalously iron- and thorium-poor (vs. the rest of the far side), suggesting it excavated lower crust or upper-mantle material.
formation_notes: Pre-Nectarian (~4.3 Ga). Probably the oldest visible impact feature on the Moon.
significance: Sample-return target for proposed missions (Endurance-A, etc.) — would deliver the oldest lunar material.
missions: Chang'e 4 (in Von Karman crater on the floor)
named_after: Bounded by the South Pole and Aitken crater (named after Robert Grant Aitken, US astronomer).

name: Mare Hertzsprung
terrain: Small basaltic patch in the floor of the giant Hertzsprung ringed basin (570 km).

name: Tycho
terrain: Sharp, fresh complex crater with terraced walls, a 1.6-km central peak, and an extensive radial bright-ray system extending up to 1500 km. Floor is hummocky impact melt.
formation_notes: Formed ~108 Ma in the Copernican period. Far younger than Copernicus despite similar size.
significance: Brightest visible crater from Earth at full moon. Its rays cross most of the southern hemisphere. Source of many secondary craters across the near side.

name: Copernicus
terrain: Large complex crater with terraced inner walls (multiple slump terraces), a central-peak cluster, and a prominent ray system. Floor has hummocky impact melt and several small craters.
formation_notes: ~800 Ma. Type-locality for the Copernican period.
significance: Centerpiece of near-side telescope views; rays reach Mare Imbrium and Mare Cognitum. Studied as the textbook complex crater.

name: Aristarchus
terrain: Bright, fresh crater perched on a 200-km-wide volcanic plateau (Aristarchus Plateau). Crater walls reveal layered rock; floor is bright with subdued central peak.
composition_notes: One of the highest thorium readings on the Moon from gamma-ray spectroscopy.
significance: Brightest large feature on the Moon — easily visible to the naked eye. The Aristarchus Plateau is rich in sinuous rilles (Schroeter's Valley) and pyroclastic deposits.
named_after: Aristarchus of Samos (Greek astronomer, c. 310–230 BC).

name: Plato
terrain: Walled plain with a remarkably flat, dark, basalt-flooded floor — almost no central peak. Sits on the northern shore of Mare Imbrium.
significance: Floor's flat darkness makes Plato a famous 'eye' on the lunar surface. Long history of telescopic observation.

name: Clavius
terrain: Massive, ancient walled plain in the southern highlands. Heavily eroded rim, flat floor punctuated by an arc of smaller progressively-younger craters (Rutherfurd, Clavius C/D/N).
significance: One of the oldest large impact features still preserved on the near side. Famous in 2001: A Space Odyssey as the Clavius Base location.

name: Plinius
terrain: Sharp-rimmed Eratosthenian crater straddling the boundary between Mare Tranquillitatis and Mare Serenitatis. Twin central peaks; floor is partially flooded by mare basalt.

name: Aristoteles
terrain: Large Imbrian-age crater on the south shore of Mare Frigoris. Terraced walls, hummocky floor, no clear central peak.

name: Kepler
terrain: Small, sharp Copernican-age crater with bright rays in Oceanus Procellarum. Walls reveal stratification.

name: Posidonius
terrain: Old, eroded crater on the northeast rim of Mare Serenitatis. Notable interior rilles (Rimae Posidonius) on the floor.

name: Theophilus
terrain: Young (Copernican-age) sharp-rimmed crater with prominent central-peak cluster. Forms a striking trio with Cyrillus and Catharina.

name: Tsiolkovsky
terrain: Most prominent feature on the lunar far side. Very dark basaltic floor in stark contrast to surrounding bright highlands; tall central peak in centre of basaltic plain.
significance: Unique among far-side craters in having a substantial mare-basalt floor — most far-side basins lack this.

name: Korolev
terrain: Large multi-ring far-side basin. Floor pockmarked with smaller craters; not flooded by basalt.

name: Apollo (crater)
terrain: Far-side double-ringed basin with partially basalt-flooded floor.

name: Hertzsprung
terrain: Multi-ring far-side basin enclosing the small Mare Hertzsprung.

name: Endymion
terrain: Old crater near the northeast limb. Floor is dark basalt fill — appears black through a telescope.
named_after: Endymion (Greek mythology — the eternally-sleeping shepherd loved by the Moon goddess Selene).

name: Atlas
terrain: Forms a famous pair with Hercules in the northeast near side. Sharp rim, hummocky floor with rilles.

name: Hercules
terrain: Twin to Atlas. Terraced walls and a small central peak.

name: Cleomedes
terrain: Old crater north of Mare Crisium. Subdued rim, floor crossed by rilles.

name: Langrenus
terrain: Prominent crater on the eastern limb. Terraced walls, central peak, partly buried in Mare Fecunditatis ejecta.

name: Petavius
terrain: Large crater near the southeast limb with a notable rille running across its floor (Rima Petavius).

name: Schickard
terrain: Walled-plain crater with a flat, partially-basalt-flooded floor. Old (pre-Nectarian).

name: Bailly
terrain: Largest near-side crater, very old. Heavily eroded rim, floor pocked with smaller craters.

name: Maginus
terrain: Old, heavily-degraded southern crater riddled with smaller later impacts.

name: Walter
terrain: Large old crater in the southern highlands.

name: Ptolemaeus
terrain: Old walled-plain crater with a flat, slightly-darker floor. Forms a famous chain with Alphonsus and Arzachel.

name: Alphonsus
terrain: Floor has a low central peak, dark-halo craters (suspected endogenic), and rilles. Site of Ranger 9 impact (1965) — returned the first close-up images of a target landing site.

name: Arzachel
terrain: Sharp-rimmed crater south of Alphonsus, with a prominent central peak and rilles.

name: Gagarin
named_after: Yuri Gagarin (Soviet cosmonaut, first human in space).

name: Shackleton
terrain: Crater straddling the lunar south pole. Interior is permanently shadowed; exterior rim catches near-constant sunlight (a 'peak of eternal light').
composition_notes: Hydrogen signal from neutron spectrometers and direct LCROSS impact (in adjacent Cabeus crater) indicate water ice in the regolith.
lighting_notes: Inside the crater, the sun never rises. Floor temperature stays below ~110 K. Rim peaks see sun for 80–90% of the year.
significance: Top candidate site for crewed return missions and ISRU (in-situ resource utilization). Artemis-3 target zone. Chandrayaan-3 (Vikram lander, 2023) landed nearby.

name: Peary
terrain: Crater very near the lunar north pole. Like Shackleton, has permanently-shadowed interior regions and rim peaks with near-constant illumination.
composition_notes: Suspected ice deposits in shadowed regions.
significance: North-pole counterpart to Shackleton. Less studied — south-pole has hosted more recent missions.

name: Faustini
terrain: South-polar crater. Floor permanently shadowed. Adjacent to Shackleton; on the proposed Artemis-3 traverse map.
significance: Active candidate for ice-prospecting rover missions.

name: Apollo 11
terrain: Flat mare-basalt plain in southwestern Mare Tranquillitatis. First crewed landing site. Visible boulders, two small craters (Little West, ~30 m), gentle rolling regolith.
composition_notes: Apollo 11 returned ilmenite-rich basalts dated to ~3.7 Ga. First samples ever returned from another world.
lighting_notes: Equatorial — lighting at the time of landing was a low morning sun for crew visibility (~10° altitude).
formation_notes: Mare basalt erupted ~3.7 Ga, then accumulated regolith from micrometeorite gardening over the next 3.7 Gy.
significance: 20 July 1969 — Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to walk on another world. Returned 21.6 kg of samples and demonstrated the feasibility of sustained human-Moon operations.

name: Apollo 12
terrain: Mare Cognitum / Oceanus Procellarum boundary. Pinpoint landing within walking distance of Surveyor 3 (which had soft-landed there 2.5 years earlier).
significance: 14 November 1969 — Pete Conrad and Alan Bean. Returned Surveyor 3 hardware components for study of long-term lunar exposure effects.

name: Apollo 14
terrain: Fra Mauro highlands — a hummocky region thought to be Imbrium impact ejecta. Crew traversed up Cone Crater rim via two-wheeled MET cart.
significance: February 1971 — Alan Shepard, Edgar Mitchell. Returned the largest Apollo single sample (Big Bertha, 8.9 kg). Shepard's golf shot.

name: Apollo 15
terrain: Hadley Rille / Apennine Mountain front. Most geologically diverse Apollo site — mare basalt, highland anorthosite, and a sinuous rille (a collapsed lava tube). First mission with the Lunar Roving Vehicle.
dominant_rock: mare basalt + anorthosite (at the Apennine front)
formed_by: multi-event: Imbrium impact rim + later basalt floods
significance: July–August 1971 — Dave Scott, Jim Irwin. Returned the Genesis Rock (anorthosite, 4.1 Ga, mantle-derived). First use of the LRV; tripled traverse range.

name: Apollo 16
terrain: Descartes Highlands — central nearside highlands. Crew tested the hypothesis that the bright highlands were volcanic; samples showed they're actually shock-modified anorthosite.
significance: April 1972 — John Young, Charles Duke. Demonstrated that lunar highlands are impact ejecta + primary anorthositic crust, not silicic volcanism. Major shift in lunar geological understanding.

name: Apollo 17
terrain: Taurus-Littrow Valley — narrow valley between mountainous highland blocks at the southeastern Mare Serenitatis rim. Three-day surface stay, 22-km LRV traverse. Mountains rise ~2–3 km above the valley floor.
composition_notes: Discovery of orange soil — pyroclastic glass beads from a fire-fountain eruption ~3.6 Ga.
formed_by: multi-event: Serenitatis basin rim + late mare basalt + pyroclastic deposits
significance: 11–14 December 1972 — last crewed lunar landing. Gene Cernan, Jack Schmitt (only scientist on the Moon). Returned 110.5 kg of samples — the largest Apollo haul.

name: Luna 9
terrain: Western Oceanus Procellarum, Marius Hills region. Featureless regolith plain with small craters and rocks.
significance: 3 February 1966 — first soft landing on the Moon. Returned the first panoramic images from the lunar surface, proving regolith would support a heavy lander.

name: Luna 16
terrain: Mare Fecunditatis, smooth basaltic plain.
significance: 20 September 1970 — first robotic sample return. Brought 101 g of soil back to Earth.

name: Luna 17
terrain: Mare Imbrium — Sinus Iridum / Promontorium Heraclides region. Lunokhod 1 rover deployed and traversed 10.5 km over 11 lunar days.
significance: 17 November 1970 — first robotic rover on another world (Lunokhod 1).

name: Luna 21
terrain: LeMonnier crater on the eastern Mare Serenitatis rim. Lunokhod 2 rover deployed (37 km traverse — record stood until 2014).
significance: January 1973 — second Lunokhod, longest extraterrestrial rover traverse for ~40 years.

name: Chang'e 4
terrain: Von Kármán crater on the floor of the South Pole–Aitken basin — the lowest, oldest region on the Moon.
lighting_notes: No direct line of sight to Earth — communication relayed via the Queqiao satellite at L2.
significance: 3 January 2019 — first soft landing on the lunar far side. Yutu-2 rover (still operational as of 2024) is the longest-active lunar rover.

name: Chang'e 5
terrain: Mons Rümker volcanic complex in northern Oceanus Procellarum. Among the youngest mare basalts on the Moon.
significance: December 2020 — first lunar sample return since Luna 24 (1976). Returned 1.7 kg, including the youngest mare basalts ever sampled, redating lunar volcanism by ~1 Gy.

name: Chandrayaan-3
terrain: High-southern-latitude highlands, near the rim of the south polar zone. Slope-rich, shadow-cast terrain.
lighting_notes: Long shadows, low sun; lander/rover sized lifetime to one lunar daylight period (~14 days).
significance: 23 August 2023 — Vikram lander touchdown made India the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon and the first to land near the south pole.

name: Surveyor 3
terrain: Surveyor crater in Oceanus Procellarum.
significance: 20 April 1967 — robotic sampler/digger lander. Visited by Apollo 12 crew 2.5 years later; pieces returned to Earth for long-term-exposure analysis.
